background: Historical context before the September 2026 claim: Metric $k$-median is the canonical fixed-budget clustering problem: choose $k$ centers to minimize total client distance. It is closely related to facility location but lacks facility-opening penalties, replacing them with a hard cardinality constraint. This hard constraint makes rounding much more delicate. After years with best ratios above $2.6$, Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson gave a $2+\epsilon$ approximation in 2025, a major improvement. The hardness lower bound remains $1+2/e\approx1.736$, and the natural LP relaxation has gap close to $2$. The question left by the 2025 result was whether the true threshold was near the hardness bound, near the LP barrier at $2$, or exactly at $2$. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities.
full_statement: In metric $k$-median, the input is a finite metric space containing a set of clients $C$, a set of candidate facilities $F$, distances $d$, and an integer $k$. The goal is to open at most $k$ facilities $S\subseteq F$ and minimize $$\sum_{j\in C} d(j,S),\qquad d(j,S)=\min_{i\in S} d(j,i).$$ Determine the optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for this problem in arbitrary metrics. The original barrier question was whether there is a $(2-\epsilon)$-approximation for some fixed $\epsilon>0$, or prove hardness approaching $2$. The standard LP relaxation has an integrality gap near $2$, so a below-$2$ algorithm would likely need a stronger relaxation or a method that escapes the usual LP barrier. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities. Under $P\ne NP$, it claims the infimum is $1+2/e$, not attainment of the exact endpoint. This record flags a claimed resolution.
open_problem: Verify the claimed $1+2/e$ infimum threshold for the specified-candidate-facility model; the original below-$2$ target is claimed resolved.
known_results: Historical context before the September 2026 claim: Jain, Mahdian, and Saberi prove NP-hardness below $1+2/e\approx1.736$ through the facility-location approximation framework. The natural LP relaxation has integrality gap at least $2-o(1)$, limiting direct LP rounding and Lagrangian-relaxation approaches. Before 2025, the best exactly-$k$ approximation ratio was $2.613$, with progress bottlenecked by bi-point rounding after facility-location-style algorithms. Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson give a $2+\epsilon$ approximation, improving the previous best ratio by avoiding the old bi-point rounding loss and combining a phased greedy modification with a stable-instance algorithm. Thus the pre-September-2026 gap was between hardness $1.736$ and algorithms arbitrarily close to $2$, with the LP barrier suggesting but not proving that $2$ may be tight. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities.

literature.synthesis: Historical algorithmic context: The old difficulty was converting facility-location-style Lagrangian guarantees into exactly $k$ centers without paying a large bi-point rounding penalty. The 2025 breakthrough shows that this penalty is not inherent up to $2+\epsilon$. That historical gap motivated searches for either a better-than-2 algorithm using a fundamentally different relaxation or a hardness proof matching the LP barrier. Because the natural LP has gap $2-o(1)$, any algorithm below $2$ probably needs stronger structure than standard LP rounding. OpenAI's September 24, 2026 research-release manuscript claims a deterministic $(1+2/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for each fixed $\epsilon>0$, in polynomial binary-input time, opening at most $k$ specified candidate facilities. The claimed method allows a constant additive facility surplus internally and removes it before output; it must not be confused with a final bicriteria guarantee.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Prioritize independent verification of the research-release manuscript, including the directed comparison inequality, bit complexity, and removal of the additive facility surplus. Investigate relaxations stronger than the standard LP, or hard instances showing $2$-hardness. Computationally compare the 2025 algorithm against LP-gap and clustering benchmark families.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed ratio below $2$ must open at most $k$ centers exactly and hold in arbitrary metrics with arbitrary client/facility sets. Bicriteria algorithms opening $k+o(k)$ centers, algorithms for Euclidean or doubling metrics only, or guarantees against strengthened assumptions such as stability do not resolve the general problem. A hardness result must rule out polynomial-time algorithms under a standard assumption and should be compared carefully with the existing $1+2/e$ lower bound and the near-$2$ LP integrality gap. The release reports Lean artifacts, but neither their execution nor alignment with the mathematical statement was checked here. The lower-bound model permits $F\ne C$; do not transfer it automatically to $F=C$.

short_statement: A 2026 research-release manuscript claims the metric $k$-median threshold $1+2/e$, via algorithms at every fixed factor above it; not independently verified here.
